pos: n. (Oliver Heywood, 1630–1702, ejected minister of Coley, itinerant preacher of the West Riding)
etymology: Latin oliva, an olive tree; Heywood, from the Lancashire place-name, the enclosed wood.
biblical_def: Oliver Heywood was a Lancashire man, trained at Trinity College, Cambridge, and settled at Coley chapel near Halifax in 1650. Ejected in 1662 and excommunicated by the ecclesiastical court in 1663, he refused to be silent and spent nearly forty years as an itinerant among the moors and valleys of the West Riding, preaching in farmhouses, barns and open fields, baptising, catechising and keeping a register of the Dissenting families of the district. He was indicted repeatedly, fined fifty pounds in 1685 and imprisoned at York, and licensed at last in 1687 and legally in 1689, when his people built him the chapel at Northowram. His diaries and the Nonconformist Register he kept are a principal source for the social history of northern Dissent. He reckoned a minister's field to be wherever hearers could be gathered, after the apostolic pattern: “have taught you publickly, and from house to house” (Act 20:20). Of his own labours he said little except that the harvest was great and the labourers few (Luk 10:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines itinerant as travelling, passing about the country, and to excommunicate as to expel from the communion of the church.
webster_full: ITIN'ERANT, a. Passing or travelling about the country; not settled in a place.
EXCOMMU'NICATE, v.t. To expel from the communion of the church, and deprive of spiritual advantages.
REG'ISTER, n. A written account or entry; a book in which entries are made.
scriptures: And how I kept back nothing that was profitable unto you, but have shewed you, and have taught you publickly, and from house to house,
Luk 10:2
Therefore said he unto them, The harvest truly is great, but the labourers are few: pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he would send forth labourers into his harvest.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Isa 50:4

The Lord GOD hath given me the tongue of the learned, that I should know how to speak a word in season to him that is weary: he wakeneth morning by morning, he wakeneth mine ear to hear as the learned.
corruption_summary: Coley's ejected minister, forty years an itinerant over the West Riding moors.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Heywood answers a quiet assumption that a ministry requires a building, a title and a salary, and that a man stripped of these is a former minister. He was excommunicated, fined and gaoled, and in the same decades he preached more sermons and baptised more children than most settled incumbents of his county.

The principle to recover is the shape of the work rather than its setting: taught “publickly, and from house to house” (Act 20:20), instant “in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2). The gift Isaiah names is a tongue trained to “speak a word in season to him that is weary” (Isa 50:4), which is a farmhouse errand as much as a pulpit one.

“The harvest truly is great, but the labourers are few” (Luk 10:2) — after the Ejection.
“be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) — forty years without a licence.

pos: n. (Matthew Sylvester, c. 1636–1708, ejected minister, Richard Baxter's colleague and literary executor)
etymology: Hebrew Mattithyahu, gift of the LORD; Latin silvestris, of the woods.
biblical_def: Matthew Sylvester was ejected in 1662 from Great Gonerby in Lincolnshire, ministered quietly through the persecuting years, and from 1692 was pastor of a Dissenting congregation at Rutland House in London, where Richard Baxter spent his last years as his assistant and preached for him without pay. Baxter made him his literary executor, and Sylvester's one great service to the church was to publish, in 1696, the Reliquiae Baxterianae — Baxter's own vast, unfinished, disorderly autobiography — printing it substantially as he found it rather than editing it into shape. He has been criticised ever since for that decision, and he was right: the book is the indispensable record of the Civil Wars, the Savoy Conference and the Ejection from inside, and a tidier version would have been a lesser one. Sylvester published little of his own. “the books, but especially the parchments” (2Ti 4:13) is the sort of charge he discharged, and the result is that a generation's works still follow it (Rev 14:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an executor as one appointed to execute a will, and a manuscript as a book or paper written with the hand.
webster_full: EXEC'UTOR, n. The person appointed by a testator to execute his will.
MAN'USCRIPT, n. A book or paper written with the hand or pen.
REL'ICS, n. That which remains; the remains of a body after decay.
scriptures: The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments.

And I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them.
Pro 10:7
The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot.
Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
corruption_summary: Baxter's executor, who printed the Reliquiae Baxterianae as he found it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Sylvester's choice raises a question of stewardship that editors still face: whether a dead man's papers are to be improved for the reader's sake or preserved for the truth's. He preserved, and took the blame for a rambling book; three centuries of historians have been glad of it.

The principle to recover is that faithfulness, not elegance, is what a steward is measured by: “it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2). Paul's own last request was for his books and parchments (2Ti 4:13), and of the dead who die in the Lord it is said that “their works do follow them” (Rev 14:13) — which is only true if someone keeps them.
roots_summary: Greek biblion (G975), a book, scroll; membrana (G3200), parchment; ergon (G2041), a work.
roots_lines: Greek biblion (G975) — a book, written scroll; 2 Timothy 4:13.
usage: “the books, but especially the parchments” (2Ti 4:13) — Baxter's papers in 1691.
“their works do follow them” (Rev 14:13) — the Reliquiae, 1696.
“The memory of the just is blessed” (Pro 10:7) — what an executor is for.

pos: n. (Samuel Annesley, c. 1620–1696, ejected lecturer of St Giles Cripplegate, grandfather of John Wesley)
etymology: Hebrew Shemuel, heard of God; Annesley, from the Nottinghamshire place-name.
biblical_def: Samuel Annesley was a Warwickshire gentleman's son, chaplain at sea to the Earl of Warwick's fleet, and from 1658 lecturer at St Giles Cripplegate in London, one of the great Puritan pulpits. Ejected in 1662, he gathered a Dissenting congregation in Little St Helen's, Bishopsgate, which he served for over thirty years through the worst of the persecution and the best of the toleration, and he edited the Morning Exercises, six volumes of sermons by the leading Nonconformist ministers which are among the most useful books the ejected men left. He had twenty-four or twenty-five children; the twenty-fifth, Susanna, married Samuel Wesley and bore John and Charles. So the household religion of a silenced Puritan lecturer stands behind the Methodist revival, by a line nobody at the time could have drawn. “His seed shall be mighty upon earth: the generation of the upright shall be blessed” (Psa 112:2). He died in 1696 saying that he was going to his God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a lecturer as a preacher in a church hired by the parish to assist the rector, and progeny as offspring, descendants.
webster_full: LEC'TURER, n. One who reads or pronounces lectures; a preacher in a church hired by the parish.
PROG'ENY, n. Offspring; race; children; descendants of the human kind.
EXER'CISE, n. Use; practice; a lesson or example for practice; religious discipline.
scriptures: His seed shall be mighty upon earth: the generation of the upright shall be blessed.
Act 2:39
For the promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off, even as many as the Lord our God shall call.

For I know him, that he will command his children and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the LORD, to do justice and judgment; that the LORD may bring upon Abraham that which he hath spoken of him.
When I call to remembrance the unfeigned faith that is in thee, which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice; and I am persuaded that in thee also.
corruption_summary: St Giles's ejected lecturer, editor of the Morning Exercises, Susanna Wesley's father.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Annesley is a standing correction to the way revivals are usually narrated, as sudden irruptions without ancestry. The Wesleys' mother was catechised in the house of a man ejected for conscience in 1662 and taught by him what she then taught them; the Methodist discipline did not come out of nowhere.

The principle to recover is the covenant reach of the promise: “the promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off” (Act 2:39). Abraham is commended because “he will command his children and his household after him” (Gen 18:19), and Timothy's faith dwelt first in his grandmother (2Ti 1:5). Three generations is the ordinary unit of God's working.
roots_summary: Hebrew zera (H2233), seed, offspring; dor (H1755), a generation; Greek epaggelia (G1860), a promise.
usage: “His seed shall be mighty upon earth” (Psa 112:2) — twenty-five children, and Susanna.
“the promise is unto you, and to your children” (Act 2:39) — the ejected household.
“which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois” (2Ti 1:5) — the line to the Wesleys.

pos: n. (Cornelius Burges, c. 1589–1665, assessor of the Westminster Assembly)
etymology: Latin Cornelius, a Roman family name, perhaps from cornu, a horn; Burges, a burgess, freeman of a town.
biblical_def: Cornelius Burges was vicar of Watford, a doctor of divinity of Oxford, and one of the two assessors of the Westminster Assembly — the officers who sat with the prolocutor and took the chair in his absence — a post he held with John White throughout its sittings. He had preached before the Long Parliament in 1640 on the day of its first fast and was deep in the counsels that produced the Assembly; he helped frame the Solemn League and Covenant and administered it to the House of Commons. He was a Presbyterian of the stricter sort, opposed the execution of the king, and spent the Commonwealth years in Wells, where he bought cathedral property and lost it at the Restoration, dying poor in 1665. His part in the Assembly was procedural rather than literary, which is why he is little read; but a body of divines sitting for over a thousand sessions needed exactly such men. “Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an assessor as one who sits by another as an assistant or adviser, and a prolocutor as the chairman of a convocation.
webster_full: ASSESS'OR, n. One appointed to sit by another; an assistant or adviser.
PROLOC'UTOR, n. The foreman or speaker of a convocation.
FAST, n. Abstinence from food; a religious mortification or humiliation.
scriptures: Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: they shall prosper that love thee.
corruption_summary: Watford's vicar, assessor of the Westminster Assembly through all its sittings.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Burges is worth an entry because the Assembly is usually remembered through the half-dozen men who wrote its best-known chapters, as though a confession were composed the way a book is. It was composed in committee, over more than a thousand sessions, by men whose chief gift was the patience to keep a disputatious house in order.

The principle to recover is that counsel is a safeguard God himself provides: “in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14). Those who labour in the word and doctrine are to be counted worthy of double honour (1Ti 5:17) — which covers the man who chairs the session as well as the man who drafts the clause.
roots_summary: Hebrew yaats (H3289), to counsel, advise; teshuah (H8668), safety; Greek presbuteros (G4245), an elder.

Greek kopiao (G2872) — to labour to weariness; 1 Timothy 5:17.
Greek poimaino from poimen (G4166) — to feed, shepherd; Acts 20:28.

“especially they who labour in the word and doctrine” (1Ti 5:17) — the Assembly's officers.
“Pray for the peace of Jerusalem” (Psa 122:6) — the fast sermon of 1640.

pos: n. (Charles Herle, 1598–1659, rector of Winwick, prolocutor of the Westminster Assembly)
etymology: Old German Karl, a free man; Herle, from a Cornish place-name.
biblical_def: Charles Herle was a Cornishman, fellow of Exeter College, Oxford, and rector of Winwick in Lancashire, then reckoned the richest living in England, which he held while serving the Westminster Assembly in London. When William Twisse died in 1646 Herle succeeded him as prolocutor and presided over the Assembly through the years in which the Confession of Faith and both Catechisms were completed and sent up to Parliament. He was a moderate Presbyterian, much used as a preacher before the Houses, a man of conciliatory temper who kept a chamber of divided and determined men at their work; the Independents, whom he opposed, spoke well of his fairness in the chair. He opposed the king's execution, retired to Winwick, and died there in 1659. Of the Assembly's output he claimed nothing personally. His office required the gift James tells every man to ask for: “If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not” (Jam 1:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a moderator as one who presides over a meeting to preserve order, and order as methodical arrangement.
webster_full: MOD'ERATOR, n. The person who presides over a meeting; one who restrains or pacifies.
OR'DER, n. Regular disposition; methodical arrangement; settled mode of proceeding.
AS'SEMBLY, n. A company of persons collected together in one place, usually for some common purpose.
scriptures: Jam 1:5
If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.

Moreover thou shalt provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, and rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens:
corruption_summary: Winwick's rector, prolocutor of the Assembly while the Confession was completed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Herle's chairmanship is a quiet rebuttal of the idea that a confession written by a committee must be a compromise document. The Assembly contained Presbyterians, Independents, Erastians and a handful of Episcopalians, and it argued for years; what came out was not a lowest common denominator but one of the most exact statements of doctrine in the language.

The principle to recover is that order is a spiritual requirement, not an administrative one: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40). Jethro's counsel to Moses was to find “able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness” (Exo 18:21) and set them to govern — which is a description of the chair as much as of the bench.

usage: “If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God” (Jam 1:5) — the prolocutor's chair.
“Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — the Assembly from 1646.
“able men, such as fear God, men of truth” (Exo 18:21) — who should sit in such a house.

pos: n. (Lazarus Seaman, d. 1675, Westminster divine, Master of Peterhouse, Hebraist and ejected minister)
etymology: Hebrew Eleazar, God is helper, through Greek Lazaros; Seaman, a mariner.
biblical_def: Lazarus Seaman was a poor man's son of Leicester who worked his way through Emmanuel College, became minister of Allhallows Bread Street in London, and was named to the Westminster Assembly, where he was one of its most active debaters and one of its best Hebraists; he argued the Presbyterian side against the Independents in the long debates on ordination and church government. Cromwell made him Master of Peterhouse, Cambridge, and he served as vice-chancellor of the university; he was ejected from both at the Restoration and from his London living in 1662, and preached afterwards to a Dissenting congregation in Meeting-House Yard, Silver Street. His library was one of the finest in England and its sale in 1676 was the first book auction held in this country. He was known for exact scholarship rather than for eloquence, in the manner the apostle prescribes: “Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to study as to apply the mind to books or learning, and a library as a collection of books belonging to a private person or to the public.
webster_full: STUD'Y, v.i. To fix the mind closely upon a subject; to apply the mind to books.
LI'BRARY, n. A collection of books belonging to a private person, or to a public institution.
AUC'TION, n. A public sale of property to the highest bidder.
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Ezr 7:10
For Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments.
Pro 2:4
If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures;
I have more understanding than all my teachers: for thy testimonies are my meditation.
corruption_summary: The Assembly's Hebraist and debater, Master of Peterhouse, twice ejected.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Seaman is a useful case against the persistent suspicion that learning and piety compete for a minister's hours. He owned the best private library in England and was ejected twice for conscience; the books did not make him pliable, and the conscience did not make him lazy.

The principle to recover is that study is commanded work and has an object: “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15). Ezra is the pattern — he “had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel” (Ezr 7:10) — and wisdom is to be searched for “as for hid treasures” (Pro 2:4), which is a description of labour, not of leisure.

“searchest for her as for hid treasures” (Pro 2:4) — the library sold in 1676.

pos: n. (Francis Rous, 1579–1659, Provost of Eton, whose psalter became the Scottish Metrical Psalms)
etymology: Latin Franciscus, a Frank, a free man; Rous, from Old French rous, red-haired.
biblical_def: Francis Rous was a Cornish gentleman, half-brother to John Pym, a member of every parliament from 1626, a lay member of the Westminster Assembly, Speaker of Barebone's Parliament and Provost of Eton under the Commonwealth. His service to the church was a book of verse. His Psalms of David in English Meeter, published in 1643 and revised at the request of the Assembly, was recommended by Parliament and then taken up by the Church of Scotland, which revised it further through committees between 1647 and 1650 and authorised the result as the metrical psalter still sung in Scottish and Presbyterian congregations. The Scottish version is so heavily reworked that Rous is a contributor rather than the author; but his was the base text, and no other versification has lasted so long in use. He also wrote devotional works of some warmth, including The Mystical Marriage. The aim of his labour was that congregations should sing Scripture itself: “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines metre as the measured arrangement of syllables in verse, and a psalter as the book of Psalms.
webster_full: ME'TER, n. Rhythmical arrangement of syllables, in verse.
PSAL'TER, n. The book of Psalms; a psalm book.
VER'SIFY, v.t. To relate or describe in verse; to turn into verse.
scriptures: Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Eph 5:19
Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
Psa 95:1
O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation.
Serve the LORD with gladness: come before his presence with singing.
corruption_summary: Eton's provost, whose versification became the Scottish Metrical Psalms of 1650.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The 1650 psalter is often dismissed as rough verse, and some of it is; the inversions and padding that scan badly on the page are the price of fitting Hebrew sense into English common metre without adding to it. That was the design: a congregation was to sing the psalm, not a poem about the psalm.

The principle to recover is the content of congregational song: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom” (Col 3:16). Whatever liberty a church takes in hymnody, a people who sing the psalms have the whole range of the spiritual life in their mouths, from “O come, let us sing unto the LORD” (Psa 95:1) to the darkest complaint.

pos: n. (John Lightfoot, 1602–1675, Westminster divine, Master of Catharine Hall, rabbinic scholar)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Lightfoot, a byname for a swift runner.
biblical_def: John Lightfoot was the greatest English rabbinic scholar of the seventeenth century and probably of any century before the nineteenth. Rector of Ashley and then of Great Munden, Master of Catharine Hall, Cambridge, and vice-chancellor of the university, he sat in the Westminster Assembly, where he kept the fullest surviving journal of its debates and argued the Erastian side on church government — the one point on which his brethren thought him wrong. His great work is the Horae Hebraicae et Talmudicae, a commentary on the Gospels, Acts, Romans and 1 Corinthians which illuminates the New Testament from the Mishnah, the Talmuds and the Midrashim, showing what a phrase of our Lord's meant to the men who first heard it. He laboured through the rabbinic literature at a time when almost no Christian did, and his notes are still cited. He studied the Jewish sources in order to read the Gospels better, which is the right order. “Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me” (Joh 5:39).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the Talmud as the book which contains the Jewish traditions, and to expound as to explain or lay open the meaning.
webster_full: TAL'MUD, n. The book which contains the Jewish traditions, the rabbinical constitutions and explications of the law.
EXPOUND', v.t. To explain; to lay open the meaning; to interpret.
RAB'BINICAL, a. Pertaining to the rabbins, or to their opinions, learning and language.
scriptures: Joh 5:39
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Pro 25:2
It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter.
corruption_summary: The Assembly's rabbinic scholar, author of the Horae Hebraicae.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Lightfoot's method has however been turned on its head by a later scholarship which uses the Jewish background to relativise the text — treating the Gospels as one more first-century document to be explained by its environment. He used the background to make the text clearer about its own claims, which is the difference between illumination and dissolution.

The principle to recover is that all the searching of Scripture terminates in a person: the writings “are they which testify of me” (Joh 5:39), and our Lord himself, “beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27). It is the glory of God to conceal a thing and the honour of the searcher to find it out (Pro 25:2).

“he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27) — his controlling text.
“the honour of kings is to search out a matter” (Pro 25:2) — forty years in the Talmuds.

pos: n. (Joseph Caryl, 1602–1673, ejected minister of St Magnus, author of the twelve-volume commentary on Job)
etymology: Hebrew Yoseph, he shall add; Caryl, from a Sussex family name.
biblical_def: Joseph Caryl was preacher to Lincoln's Inn, a member of the Westminster Assembly, one of the ministers sent by Parliament to attend the king at Holmby and to Uxbridge, and from 1650 rector of St Magnus the Martyr by London Bridge, from which he was ejected in 1662. He gathered an Independent congregation afterwards which John Owen joined to in 1673. He also served as one of the commissioners for the propagation of the gospel in New England and helped procure the printing of Eliot's Indian Bible. His monument is a work of extraordinary length: an exposition of the book of Job in twelve quarto volumes, published between 1643 and 1666, the largest commentary on a single book of Scripture ever produced in English. It is the fruit of over twenty years of weekly lecturing on Job, and it was written through the Civil Wars, the Commonwealth, the Restoration and his own ejection, which is perhaps why Job suited him. “For I know that my redeemer liveth” (Job 19:25) is the centre of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a commentary as an exposition of the sense of an author, and patience as the suffering of afflictions with a calm mind.
webster_full: COM'MENTARY, n. A comment or exposition; an explanation of the meaning of an author.
PA'TIENCE, n. The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity or provocation with a calm, unruffled temper.
EXPOSI'TION, n. Explanation; interpretation; a laying open of the sense.
scriptures: For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth:
Jam 5:11
Behold, we count them happy which endure. Ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy.
Job 1:21
And said, Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.
Rom 15:4
For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.
corruption_summary: The ejected rector of St Magnus, whose Job commentary ran to twelve volumes.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Twelve volumes on Job looks like a monument to excess until one notices when they were written: a man lecturing weekly on the sufferings of a righteous sufferer, through two decades in which his country tore itself apart and he lost his own living at the end of it. The scale is not scholarly vanity but pastoral need.

The principle to recover is that the Scriptures of patience are given for use: “whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope” (Rom 15:4). Job's own two confessions frame the book — “the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD” (Job 1:21) and “I know that my redeemer liveth” (Job 19:25).

pos: n. (John Arrowsmith, 1602–1659, Westminster divine, Master of St John's and then Trinity, Cambridge)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Arrowsmith, a maker of arrows.
biblical_def: John Arrowsmith was a Northumbrian, fellow of St Catharine's, minister at King's Lynn, and a member of the Westminster Assembly, where he was reckoned among its ablest theologians. He was made Master of St John's College in 1644 and of Trinity in 1653, and Regius Professor of Divinity at Cambridge in 1651. His Tactica Sacra and the posthumous Theanthropos, an unfinished exposition of the first chapter of John's gospel, show a mind trained in the old scholastic method and bent entirely on the person of Christ: the incarnation, he argued, is the point at which every other doctrine is either secured or lost. He was blind in one eye from a childhood accident with an arrow, which his friends thought a providence suited to his name. He died at Cambridge in 1659 and so did not live to be ejected. His whole divinity turned on one verse: “And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us” (Joh 1:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the incarnation as the act of assuming flesh, and a mystery as something above human intelligence, a truth revealed in Scripture.
webster_full: INCARNA'TION, n. The act of clothing with flesh; the union of the divine nature with the human.
MYS'TERY, n. A profound secret; something above human intelligence; in Scripture, a truth revealed.
DIVIN'ITY, n. The science of divine things; theology.

And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.

And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory.

For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
corruption_summary: The Assembly's Cambridge theologian, whose divinity turned on the incarnation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Arrowsmith is worth reading against a modern instinct that treats the incarnation chiefly as a statement about God's solidarity with human suffering and leaves the two natures unexamined. He held that everything hangs on the precise terms: that the Word was made flesh without ceasing to be the Word, and that the whole of salvation is in that clause.

The principle to recover is that the mystery is confessed and not resolved: “without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh” (1Ti 3:16). In Christ “are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col 2:3), and the light we are given is “the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2Co 4:6).
